methodology.aggregation: mean_per_question; fleet_composite = mean(agent_means); recommendation from composite thresholds

feature.name: Pricing Change
feature.description:
current pricing tiers are 0$(limited use case) and 20$(full access)
which we are not changing to 20$(full access with limits on total discounts) and 50$(full access + no limits)

perQuestion.text: How likely are you to continue using Fly Upsell & Cross Sell on the new $20/month plan that limits total discounts, on a scale of 0 to 100?
How likely are you to upgrade to the new $50/month plan for full access with no limits on total discounts, on a scale of 0 to 100?
How important is having no limits on total discounts to your Shopify store's upsell and bundle strategy, on a scale of 0 to 100?
How satisfied would you be with the new pricing structure ($20 with discount limits, $50 unlimited) compared to the current $0 and $20 tiers, on a scale of 0 to 100?
How likely are you to recommend Fly Upsell & Cross Sell to other Shopify Advanced or Plus merchants after this pricing change, on a scale of 0 to 100?

themes.label: Pricing feels like a hike/repackaging of prior $20 access
Reluctant upgrade to $50 for unlimited discounts
Low-volume/stable merchants staying on $20 and rejecting $50

representativeQuotes.text: The limit on the $20 tier is a non-starter for BFCM — I run stacks of bundles, tiered discounts, and free-gift thresholds all through November, so I'd have to move to the $50 plan whether I like it or not. I'll pay it because a discount interruption during peak weekend costs far more than $30, but the pricing rollout feels like my current plan is being repackaged and resold to me at 2.5x. I'd still recommend it to other advanced merchants, with a clear warning to budget for the $50 tier before the holiday rush.

I’d upgrade to the $50 plan for BFCM because unlimited discounts are non-negotiable when running bundles, tiered offers, and BOGO at peak scale. The new limit on the $20 tier is a real problem, and the price jump will be tough to justify to my budget-conscious exec, so I’d only recommend this to high-volume merchants who can absorb the $50 plan.

I can’t risk discount limits during BFCM, so I’d grudgingly upgrade to the $50 plan to keep campaigns running. But I’m unhappy that the old $20 full-access tier is being squeezed, and I wouldn’t enthusiastically recommend the new pricing to other advanced merchants.

I’d almost certainly move to the $50 plan because unlimited discounts are essential for my promotional calendar, but I’m frustrated that I now have to pay more to keep the full access I already had. I’d recommend it to other high-volume Shopify merchants, with the clear warning that the $20 tier will choke serious bundling and cross-sell strategies.

I'd almost certainly upgrade to the $50 plan because my promotional calendar and bundle strategy can't afford discount limits. The $20 tier with limits would create constant friction, so I'm not happy that full access now costs $50. I'd recommend it to other high-volume Shopify merchants, but only if they're ready to pay for the top tier.

Unlimited discount usage is exactly what our promotional calendar needs, so we'd almost certainly move to the $50 tier rather than ration campaigns on the capped $20 plan. That said, going from full access at $20 to paying $50 for what we already had feels like a penalty for running a lot of promotions, so I'd adopt it reluctantly and would be lukewarm recommending it to similar merchants.

I’d likely stay on the $20 plan because I don’t run enough discounts to need unlimited capacity. The new $50 tier feels unnecessary for my store, so I’d only consider it if my campaigns grew enough to hit the limits. I’m not thrilled that the $20 plan now has caps, but as long as they don’t affect me, I’ll keep using it.

I'd stay on the $20 plan because my store doesn't need unlimited discounts, and I'm not paying $50 just to remove limits. The change makes the $20 tier less generous than before, so I'd only recommend it with caution to similar cost-sensitive merchants.

I’d stick with the $20 plan as long as the discount limits don’t get in my way, since my store only runs a few bundles and discounts. I wouldn’t upgrade to $50 for unlimited discounts I don’t need, so I’m not thrilled that full access now costs more. I’d be hesitant to recommend it to similar merchants unless they actually hit the limits.

I’d probably stay on the $20 plan if the new discount limits don’t affect my small set of proven bundles and discounts. But I don’t like that the plan I already trusted now feels restricted, and I wouldn’t upgrade to $50 unless my business genuinely grows into needing unlimited discounts.

I'd stay on the $20 plan since my bundles and discounts are already set up and I rarely hit any caps, but paying the same price for a plan that now has limits feels like a quiet downgrade. The $50 tier is irrelevant to me because I don't need more promotional capacity, so I wouldn't recommend this change to other stable stores unless their discount volume actually grows.

As a stable merchant, I don't need unlimited discounts, so I'll likely stay on the $20 plan if the limits don't disrupt my existing bundles. However, the pricing change feels like a downgrade or a forced upsell, so I'm not happy about it and wouldn't recommend it to peers.

As a BFCM power user, discount limits are a non-starter during peak. I’d move to the $50 plan for unlimited discounts, but I’m frustrated that the previous $20 full-access tier is now capped. I’d recommend it only with the caveat that serious holiday campaigns need the $50 tier.

executiveSummary: The provided recommendation is iterate. The proposed pricing split produces a polarized response: the $50 unlimited tier is compelling for high-volume BFCM and promotional merchants, while the capped $20 tier is widely perceived as a downgrade, repackaging, or forced upsell. Fleet composite mean is 46.5 and median is 48.6; satisfaction with new pricing is low at 31.4, and recommendation likelihood is 43.1. Persona_1 and persona_2 show high upgrade intent to $50, with upgrade means of 90.4 and 88.3 and near-max importance of unlimited discounts at 96.4 and 94.3, but they adopt reluctantly and with caveats. Persona_3 and new_install stay on $20, with continue means of 86.2 and 73.2, while rejecting $50 and reacting negatively to the caps. The path forward should address the $20 limit and repackaging concerns before broad rollout.
strengths: The $50 unlimited plan addresses a real need: importanceOfUnlimitedDiscounts has mean 57.4 and median 93, with 13 of 25 agents scoring 80-100.
High-volume BFCM and promotional merchants are willing to upgrade: upgradeToFiftyForUnlimited means are 90.4 for persona_1 (count 7) and 88.3 for persona_2 (count 6).
The $20 capped plan retains low-volume merchants: continueOnTwentyWithLimits means are 86.2 for persona_3 (count 6) and 73.2 for new_install (count 6).
Even reluctant upgraders often conditionally recommend the product to other high-volume Shopify merchants, provided they budget for the $50 tier before peak promotional periods.
blockers: The $20 plan discount limits/caps are a negative theme with approxCount 25; persona_1 continueOnTwentyWithLimits is only 16.4, indicating caps are a non-starter during BFCM and heavy promotional periods.
Pricing feels like a hike or repackaging of prior $20 full access, a negative theme with approxCount 24; merchants say the previous $20 tier is now capped and full access costs $50.
Satisfaction with the new pricing is low: mean 31.4, median 30, and 20 of 25 agents scored in the 20-39 range.
Recommendation likelihood after the pricing change is moderate-to-low: mean 43.1, with no scores in the 80-100 range.
Low-volume and stable merchants reject the $50 tier: upgradeToFiftyForUnlimited means are 8.8 for persona_3 and 11.3 for new_install; they see the change as a quiet downgrade or forced upsell.
The response is structurally polarized: upgradeToFiftyForUnlimited has 12 agents in 0-19 and 13 agents in 80-100, so means hide opposite reactions.
Conditional recommendations and caveats are a mixed theme with approxCount 11; willingness to recommend depends heavily on merchant volume and whether they already hit discount limits.
segmentInsights: The BFCM Campaign Power User (persona_1, count 7, compositeMean 56.9): continueOnTwentyWithLimits 16.4 versus upgradeToFiftyForUnlimited 90.4 and importanceOfUnlimitedDiscounts 96.4. Caps are treated as a peak-season non-starter; they will grudgingly move to $50 and recommend only with a clear budget warning.

The Promotion Strategist (persona_2, count 6, compositeMean 58.4): continueOnTwentyWithLimits 27.0, upgradeToFiftyForUnlimited 88.3, and importanceOfUnlimitedDiscounts 94.3. Unlimited discounts are essential for their promotional calendars, but adoption is reluctant because full access now costs $50.

The Efficient Small-Scale Merchant (persona_3, count 6, compositeMean 38.3): continueOnTwentyWithLimits 86.2, upgradeToFiftyForUnlimited 8.8, and importanceOfUnlimitedDiscounts 15.3. They stay on $20 if caps do not bite, reject $50, and are cautious about recommending the change.

The Stable, Low-Change Merchant (new_install, count 6, compositeMean 30.8): continueOnTwentyWithLimits 73.2, upgradeToFiftyForUnlimited 11.3, importanceOfUnlimitedDiscounts 17.2, and recommendAfterPricingChange 25.7. They perceive the new $20 caps as a quiet downgrade or forced upsell and show low recommendation intent.
dataLimitations: Synthetic agent panel of 25 agents; all 25 completed and 0 are missing. Findings are directional and not observed market behavior.
Archetype counts are small, ranging from 6 to 7 per segment, so segment-level means are sensitive and not statistically robust.
Results rely on self-reported likelihood scores. There is no real payment, usage, churn, or conversion data, and the actual discount-limit thresholds are unspecified.

Several distributions are bimodal or highly polarized. upgradeToFiftyForUnlimited has 12 agents in 0-19 and 13 in 80-100, while importanceOfUnlimitedDiscounts has median 93 versus mean 57.4; averages mask opposing reactions.
The target market is limited to Shopify Advanced and Plus merchants. Results may not generalize to other Shopify plans, lower-volume stores, or non-Shopify ecommerce platforms.
Methodology reports fleet composite mean 46.5, median 48.6, and percentLikelyAdopt 0; adoption interpretation should account for threshold-based aggregation.
Themes are approximate counts and representative quotes are illustrative synthetic examples; they should not be treated as exact prevalence or exhaustive qualitative evidence.
